Requiem: this game actually realized the personal horror that Masquerade was originally conceived as. The two Sects have been replaced with five Covenants that are less openly hostile to each other, allowing for more nuanced political posturing. Vampires have unreliable memories and there is no agreed upon origin for vampires. The major antagonists are a race of shadowy, owl like creatures that claim a distant ancestry with vampires and detest Humanity. **Werewolf** Apocalypse: The end of the world is coming and chances are good that its too late to do anything to stop it. Werewolves are warriors created by Gaia to be her defenders, and the they are here to stop the Wyrm from destroying all existence. Werewolves are divided into 13 different tribes who can barely cooperate together at the best of times. Tends to center around lots of enviromental and misanthropic themes with a healthy dose of existential nihilism.  Forsaken: Werewolves are created by the union of two spirits in prehistoric times: Mother Moon, the spirit of the Moon, and Father Wolf, the ultimate predator. Eventually Father Wolf grew sick and old and so some werewolves decided he needed to be put down. Those who killed him became Forsaken, saddled with the responsibility of policing the boundaries between the world of flesh and the world of spirits for all time. Those who did not are Pure, cursed by Mother Moon for a crime they didn't commit and are dedicated to the destruction of the Forsaken. In this game werewolves are the ultimate hunters rather than warriors, the game is focused more on the pack then on larger global conflicts, and everything is painted in shades of grey rather than an obvious, we're good guys let's kill the bad guys. **Mage** Ascension: Reality is not fixed, but based on the Consensus of mankind's collective unconsciousness. A few individuals are able to awaken to this fact and then can shape reality to suite their own whims, but if the Sleepers see acts of magic that violate their idea of how the world should work the mage suffers from Paradox. The mystically focused Council of Mystic Traditions and the science focused Technocracy are locked in a centuries long battle to determine the nature of reality. Awakening: The world has Fallen due to the hubris of men. The world we think is real is a pale shadow of a much grander reality that is cut off from us by a reality destroying chasm called the Abyss. Only five watchtowers in the Supernal Realms can cut through the Abyss and call out to the souls of certain individuals, who become mages. Mages are driven by their gnosis to uncover mysteries and search for symbols of the Supernal in the Fallen World. Paradox happens when mages draw on more power than they can handle and draw on the attention of the Abyss. **Ghosts** Oblivion: You're dead and because of your angst, unfinished business, and straight up refusal to accept death, you failed to pass on to the true afterlife and are stuck in a purgatory called the Shadowlands. Also you have an evil voice inside your head that will tempt you into giving it more and more power so it can turn you into a servant of the reality destroying maelstrom called Oblivion. Welcome to the bleakest, most depressing game ever made. Sin-Eaters: You almost died, but at the precipice of the afterlife a strange ghost/spirit hybrid made a deal with you: it can bring you make to life, make you stronger, even give you supernatural powers, but in return it gets to have a ride along inside your head and your body. Also that new voice inside you is kind of weird and doesn't quite get things like humanity or morality. **Changeling** Dreaming: So faeries used to be real and they used to have a whole world of their own, but it's dead now and all the faeries along with it, except for the portions of the souls of a few faeries who constantly get reincarnated into human bodies. The Lost: So you were once an ordinary Joe (or Jane) until one of the all-powerful True Fae abducted you and held you as slave and prisoner in their nightmare dream world of Arcadia. For starters we would have to ask ourselves: what is *that game* about? Well from my reading it's about being a cursed monster who has to feed off humanity to slake unnatural hungers while being in turn hunted by the few humans who are aware that you exist. This sounds familiar because as a concept it was already executed to great commercial and critical success by *that other vampire game* in 1991. Okay so *that game* isn't treading fresh ground but the problem like I said before is that *that game* is in denial about its own nature and it pretends that its something like *that werewolf game* or *that ghost game* where sure we might be monsters, but we're good monsters trying to make the world better. Except in the werewolf games you're either trying to save the world from the apocalypse or you're trying to protect the world from amoral predatory spirits. *That werewolf game* gets to turn what would otherwise be slavering monstrosities into compelling protagonists by successfully making the case that they are necessary and despite their nastier elements, they do make the world a better place. *That game* falls at this hurdle, I don't get the sense that Beasts "teaching a lesson" angle of what they do is anything other than a filmsy, post-hoc rationalization for being monsters and that sucks. Frankly their methods are terrible, all they can do is instill avoidance behavior and there's no guarantee their victims might even understand there's a lesson there at all. Vampires don't go around telling themselves that ghouling and turning people into blood dolls is for their own good, they do it because vampires are monsters and humans are their prey. Both *vampire games* acknowledge that vampires are not nice people, and the ones who try to be are struggling hard against that nature. So like I said the first step is to drop the "lessons" bit, or keep it but present it as a weak excuse Beasts who are uncomfortable with their nature use to deny what they really have become. The rules on feeding don't support it anyway, an Anakim Tyrant can amass a Texas Chainsaw Massacre reputation as a hillbilly monster who collects torsos and the only lesson he would need to teach is "don't be outside when the guy with the womanskin mask comes to harvest torsos". So with that angle gone *that game* is sort of stuck getting too close to *vampire's* territory, it's a game of personal horror where the horror comes from facing what you are and what you have to do to keep worse things from happening. It's selling point is that while *vampire* pidgeon-holds you into being a vampire, Beasts can be anything.  The other major elephant in the room that needs to be addressed is Heroes. They're a mess and we all know it and I don't need to explain why. So let's just make them more sympathetic, since sympathetic villains are a sign of a good writer (take notes McFarland). The first step to fixing them is acknowledging that Heroes are the result of Beasts failing at being good Beasts (a good Beast is not a "teacher of wisdom" but a Beast who keeps their Horror feed responsibly and is not too proud of some of the things they have to do as a result). Heroes are born from Beasts screwing up and letting their Horrors ruin another person. A Beast should confront a Hero with a mixture of shame and disappointment, not scorn and ridicule. Also, Heroes should not be universally assholes, they can be obsessed, monomaniacal, and self-involved, but they do have a point: monsters are real and they ruined my life. They turned me into an emotional train wreak (remember low Integrity doesn't mean you're a bad person, it means you literally cannot even in the face of spooky shit) and I want, no need, payback. When I first read about Heroes when *that game* was being pitched I thought about David from *that book series*. Yes, David was a selfish, narcissistic little brat who nearly killed off the protagonists and damned Earth to the Yeerks, but he was also a product of the Animorph's screwing up and inflicting their nightmare life onto a scared kid who wasn't mentally or emotionally prepared for it. David was still one of the biggest threats the Animorphs ever faced, but the tragedy of his situation is what made his story stick with me for over 20 years. So that's my take on it. Oh also that rule about how Beasts get a +2 bonus and an automatic door unlock when dealing with other supernatural splats can go right off and fuck itself. How to Fix Beast TL;DR: drop the "we're doing it for your own good" attitude, make Beasts sympathetic but making them afraid of their own Horrors and what their Horrors can do if unchecked, and make Heroes less Gaston and more David from *that book series*.
